extracted.intended_audience: K-12 teachers and writing assessors (educators and classroom scorers)
extracted.subtask_description: A K–12 classroom scoring rubric (the 6+1 Traits) for assessing student writing across seven dimensions (Ideas, Organization, Voice, Word Choice, Sentence Fluency, Conventions, Presentation) using a 1–5 scale with descriptive anchors and behaviorally‑specific indicators.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scoring continuum / scale definitions
rubrics_metrics.description: Defines the overall rating scale and what each numeric level means (including a top 'WOW! Exceeds expectations' label).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: WOW! Exceeds expectations. 5 STRONG: shows control and skill in this trait; many strengths present. 4 EFFECTIVE: on balance, the strengths outweigh the weaknesses; a small amount of revision is needed. 3 DEVELOPING: strengths and need for revision are about equal; about half-way home. 2 EMERGING: need for revision outweighs strengths; isolated moments hint at what the writer has in mind. 1 NOT YET: a bare beginning; writer not yet showing any control.

rubrics_metrics.name: IDEAS
rubrics_metrics.description: Clarity and focus of the paper; relevance and quality of details that enrich the central theme.
rubrics_metrics.guidance:
Level 5 (Strong): This paper is clear and focused. It holds the reader's attention. Relevant anecdotes and details enrich the central theme. A. Topic is narrow and manageable. B. Relevant, telling, quality details give reader important information beyond the obvious. C. Reasonably accurate details support main ideas. D. Writer appears to write from knowledge or experience; ideas are fresh and original. E. Reader’s questions are anticipated and answered. F. Insight is an indicator of high-level performance (not required).
Level 3 (Developing): The writer is beginning to define the topic, development is basic or general. A. Topic is fairly broad but direction is observable. B. Support is attempted but doesn't flesh out key issues/storyline. C. Ideas are reasonably clear but may lack detail, personalization, accuracy, or expansion. D. Writer draws on knowledge/experience but has trouble moving from general to specific. E. Reader is left with questions; more info needed. F. Writer generally stays on topic but does not develop a clear theme.
Level 1 (Not yet): Paper has no clear sense of purpose or central theme; reader must infer meaning from sketchy/missing details. A. Writer still searching for topic or hasn't decided main idea. B. Information limited/unclear or length inadequate. C. Idea is simple restatement or answer with little/no detail. D. Writer hasn't defined topic in meaningful, personal way. E. Everything seems equally important; reader can't sift significance. F. Text may be repetitious or read like disconnected thoughts with no point.

rubrics_metrics.name: ORGANIZATION
rubrics_metrics.description: How order, structure, pacing, transitions, and paragraphing shape and move the reader through the text to support the central idea or theme.
rubrics_metrics.guidance:
Level 5 (Strong): Organization enhances and showcases central idea/theme; order, structure, and presentation are compelling and move the reader. A. Inviting introduction; satisfying conclusion with closure. B. Thoughtful transitions show idea connections. C. Details fit and sequencing is logical/effective. D. Pacing well controlled—knows when to elaborate or move on. E. Title (if desired) is original and captures central theme. F. Choice of structure matches purpose/audience with effective paragraph breaks.
Level 3 (Developing): Organizational structure is strong enough to move reader without too much confusion. A. Recognizable introduction and conclusion (may be weak). B. Transitions sometimes work; sometimes connections unclear. C. Sequencing shows some logic but not consistently controlled; structure may be predictable. D. Pacing fairly controlled but sometimes uneven. E. Title may be present but uninspired. F. Organization sometimes supports main point with attempted paragraphing.
Level 1 (Not yet): Writing lacks clear direction; ideas/details/events strung loosely with no internal structure. A. No real lead or conclusion. B. Connections confusing or absent. C. Sequencing random. D. Pacing awkward. E. No title or title does not reflect content. F. Organizational problems make main point/story hard to understand; little/no paragraphing.

rubrics_metrics.name: VOICE
rubrics_metrics.description: The writer's connection with the audience and the sense of individual, compelling presence in the writing; appropriateness of tone for purpose and audience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance:
Level 5 (Strong): Writer speaks directly to reader in an individual, compelling, engaging way with awareness of audience and purpose. A. Strong connection through intriguing focus, relevant details, and natural language. B. Purpose reflected in choice of compelling content and arrangement. C. Writer takes risks with personal details revealing the person behind the words. D. Expository/persuasive writing shows commitment and builds credibility. E. Narrative writing is personal, engaging, and thought‑provoking.
Level 3 (Developing): Writer seems sincere but not fully engaged; writing has discernable purpose but is not compelling. A. Attempts to connect earnestly but is somewhat impersonal. B. Aware of purpose; attempts to select content/structure to reflect it. C. Occasionally reveals personal details but avoids risk. D. Expository/persuasive writing lacks consistent engagement and fails to build credibility. E. Narrative is sincere but lacks unique/individual perspective.
Level 1 (Not yet): Writer seems indifferent; writing lacks purpose and audience engagement. A. Ideas and language fail to connect. B. No clear purpose; style doesn't match content. C. Writing is risk-free and reveals nothing about author. D. Expository/persuasive writing is lifeless or inaccurate. E. Narrative development too limited for discernible point of view.

rubrics_metrics.name: WORD CHOICE
rubrics_metrics.description: Precision, interest, and appropriateness of vocabulary; power and vividness of words and phrases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance:
Level 5 (Strong): Words convey intended message precisely, interestingly, naturally; language is powerful and engaging. A. Words are specific and accurate—meaning is clear. B. Striking words/phrases catch the eye and linger. C. Language and phrasing are natural and appropriate for audience. D. Lively verbs add energy; specific nouns/modifiers add depth. E. Choices enhance meaning and clarify understanding. F. Precision is obvious—just the right word/phrase is used.
Level 3 (Developing): Language is functional though lacks energy; meaning is generally understandable. A. Words are adequate/correct and support meaning. B. Familiar words communicate but rarely captivate. C. Attempts at colorful language sometimes overreach (thesaurus overload). D. Writing marked by passive verbs, everyday nouns, mundane modifiers. E. Words/phrases functional with a few fine moments. F. Language looks like first-thought choices; may need refinement.
Level 1 (Not yet): Limited vocabulary or lack of word search; words distract or obscure meaning. A. Words nonspecific/distracting so meaning is limited. B. Language problems leave reader wondering. C. Audience not considered; language used incorrectly. D. Limited vocabulary/misused parts of speech impair understanding. E. Words/phrases unimaginative and lifeless. F. Jargon or clichés distract; redundancy is problematic.

rubrics_metrics.name: SENTENCE FLUENCY
rubrics_metrics.description: Flow, rhythm, cadence, and variety of sentence structure; how well sentences invite expressive oral reading.
rubrics_metrics.guidance:
Level 5 (Strong): Writing has easy flow, rhythm, and cadence; sentences are well-built and varied, inviting expressive oral reading. A. Sentences constructed to underscore and enhance meaning. B. Sentences vary in length and structure; fragments used stylistically; dialogue natural. C. Purposeful and varied sentence beginnings add energy. D. Creative and appropriate connectives show relationships between thoughts. E. Writing has cadence; writer considered sound as well as meaning. (First oral reading is a breeze.)
Level 3 (Developing): Text hums along with steady beat—more pleasant/businesslike than musical. A. Sentences may not be artful but get the job done. B. Sentences usually constructed correctly and hang together. C. Some variety in sentence beginnings is attempted. D. Reader sometimes must hunt for connecting clues (however, therefore, for example, etc.). E. Parts invite expressive reading; others are stiff or awkward.
Level 1 (Not yet): Reader must practice to give a fair interpretive reading; more than one problem present. A. Sentences choppy, incomplete, rambling or awkward; phrasing unnatural. B. Little to no “sentence sense”; sentences don't hang together. C. Many sentences begin the same way or follow monotonous patterns. D. Endless connectives or lack of connectives creates jumble. E. Text does not invite expressive oral reading.

rubrics_metrics.name: CONVENTIONS
rubrics_metrics.description: Control of standard writing conventions (spelling, punctuation, capitalization, grammar, usage, paragraphing) used to enhance readability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance:
Level 5 (Strong): Writer demonstrates good grasp of conventions; errors are few and piece is nearly publishable. A. Spelling generally correct, even on difficult words. B. Punctuation accurate (even creative) and guides reader. C. Consistent capitalization skills. D. Grammar and usage correct and contribute to clarity/style. E. Paragraphing sound and reinforces organization. F. Writer may manipulate conventions for stylistic effect successfully. Note: GRADES 7 AND UP ONLY — writing must be sufficiently complex to show skill in a wide range of conventions; for younger writers, control over age-appropriate conventions is expected.
Level 3 (Developing): Reasonable control over a limited range of conventions; errors sometimes distract. A. Spelling usually correct or reasonably phonetic on common words; difficult words problematic. B. End punctuation usually correct; internal punctuation sometimes missing/wrong. C. Most capitalization correct; sophisticated capitalization spotty. D. Grammar/usage problems not serious enough to distort meaning but not always correct. E. Paragraphing attempted but may run together or be misplaced. F. Moderate editing would be required to polish the text.
Level 1 (Not yet): Errors in conventions repeatedly distract and make text difficult to read. A. Frequent spelling errors, even on common words. B. Punctuation often missing or incorrect. C. Capitalization random. D. Grammar/usage errors noticeable, frequent, and affect meaning. E. Paragraphing missing, irregular, or so frequent it doesn't reflect structure. F. Reader must read once to decode then again for meaning; extensive editing required.

rubrics_metrics.name: PRESENTATION
rubrics_metrics.description: Physical appearance and overall presentation of the piece as a component of writing quality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Trait listed in the 6+1 framework (Presentation) — the fetched page lists Presentation among the traits but did not include the detailed rubric descriptors in the provided text. No additional level-specific guidance was present in the available content.
